title: The river crossing
text:
The monsoon had lasted for three weeks, and the river that ran past Wayan's village was no longer a gentle stream. It was a brown, roaring monster, swollen with rainwater and carrying branches from the hills.

Every morning, Wayan and his sister Ketut crossed the old bamboo bridge to reach school on the far bank. This morning, as they stood at the edge, Ketut gasped. The water was licking at the planks, and the bridge shuddered with every surge.

"We cannot cross," said Ketut firmly. "We will go home."

Wayan shook his head. "The test is today. If we miss it, we fail the whole term." He took a step onto the bridge. The bamboo creaked like an old door. A cold knot twisted in his stomach, but he kept walking.

Halfway across, a large log crashed into the support. The whole bridge lurched. Wayan fell to his knees and clung to the rail as the brown water foamed beneath him. For a moment he could not move. Then he heard Ketut shouting from the bank, her voice thin against the roar. "Wayan! Come back! Crawl, crawl slowly!"

He did exactly that. Inch by inch, hands gripping the wet bamboo, he crept backwards until his feet touched solid ground. He lay on the grass, shaking, while Ketut hugged him so tightly that he could hardly breathe.

"I was foolish," he whispered.

"You were brave," she corrected him gently, "but bravery needs good sense as well."

That afternoon, the village headman rang the iron bell. The men gathered with ropes and fresh bamboo and began to repair the bridge. Wayan and Ketut carried water and tools for them all day. When the river finally fell, the teacher walked all the way from the school to the bank. "The test can wait," she said, smiling. "The two of you matter more."

Wayan looked at the new bridge, strong and pale in the evening light, and realised that he had learned something no test could measure.
